title: Das Bürle
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 61. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng/giengen, anfieng, thun, frißt, todt und ward).
about: KHM 61, a trickster tale with no moral in it whatever. The one poor man in a village of rich ones sets a wooden calf out to graze on the common, and out of that first small fraud the story climbs: a raven passed off as a soothsayer, a parson shut in a cupboard, a shepherd sealed into a barrel, and at last a sky full of little clouds that the peasants take for sheep. The spelling is the 1857 edition’s, so you will meet gieng, empfieng, Thüre, todt, Reichthum and Vortheil.

sentences.t: Es war ein Dorf, darin saßen lauter reiche Bauern und nur ein armer, den nannten sie das Bürle (Bäuerlein).
sentences.l: There was a village; in it sat nothing but rich peasants and only one poor one, whom they called das Bürle (the little peasant).
sentences.i: There was a village in which all the peasants were rich but one, and him they called Bürle — the little peasant.
sentences.n: Bürle is the southern diminutive of Bauer, and Grimm glosses it himself in the 1857 text as Bäuerlein. Because it is a diminutive it is grammatically neuter — das Bürle — so the tale calls a grown man es, ihm and sein, an “it” for a man that English cannot copy — though it slips back into masculine er often enough (“Er hatte nicht einmal eine Kuh,” “kam er an eine Mühle”). lauter here = nothing but.

sentences.t: Er hatte nicht einmal eine Kuh und noch weniger Geld eine zu kaufen: und er und seine Frau hätten so gern eine gehabt.
sentences.l: He had not even a cow and still less money to buy one: and he and his wife would so gladly have had one.
sentences.i: He had not even a cow, and still less the money to buy one; and he and his wife would so dearly have liked to have one.
sentences.n: eine stands alone for eine Kuh, the noun dropped and its gender left in the ending. “hätten … gehabt” is the past subjunctive: would so gladly have had one.

sentences.t: Einmal sprach er zu ihr „hör, ich habe einen guten Gedanken, da ist unser Gevatter Schreiner, der soll uns ein Kalb aus Holz machen und braun anstreichen, daß es wie ein anderes aussieht, mit der Zeit wirds wohl groß und gibt eine Kuh.“
sentences.l: One time he spoke to her “listen, I have a good thought: there is our Gevatter the joiner — he shall make us a calf out of wood and paint it brown, so that it looks like any other; in time it will surely grow big and make a cow.”
sentences.i: One day he said to her: “Listen, I have a good idea. There is our neighbour the joiner — let him make us a calf out of wood and paint it brown so that it looks like any other; in time it will grow big and turn into a cow.”
sentences.n: Gevatter is the godparent bond between two households — a standing obligation, not mere friendliness; “unser Gevatter Schreiner” is the joiner who stands godfather to their child. anstreichen = to paint over, separable. wirds = wird es. “gibt eine Kuh” — gives, that is, yields, turns out to be a cow.

sentences.t: Der Frau gefiel das auch, und der Gevatter Schreiner zimmerte und hobelte das Kalb zurecht, strich es an, wie sichs gehörte, und machte es so, daß es den Kopf herab senkte, als fräße es.
sentences.l: The wife liked that too, and the Gevatter joiner carpentered and planed the calf into shape, painted it as was fitting, and made it so that it sank its head down, as if it were feeding.
sentences.i: The wife liked the plan well enough, and the joiner sawed and planed the calf into shape, painted it as it ought to be, and made it so that it hung its head down as if it were feeding.
sentences.n: gefallen takes the dative: literally “that pleased to the wife.” “wie sichs gehörte” = as was proper. fräße is the subjunctive of fressen, which is the verb for an animal’s eating — hence “as if it were grazing.”

sentences.t: Wie die Kühe des andern Morgens ausgetrieben wurden, rief das Bürle den Hirt herein und sprach „seht, da hab ich ein Kälbchen, aber es ist noch klein und muß noch getragen werden.“
sentences.l: When the cows were driven out the next morning, the Bürle called the herdsman in and spoke “see, here I have a little calf, but it is still small and must still be carried.”
sentences.i: When the cows were driven out the next morning, Bürle called the herdsman in and said: “Look, here I have a little calf; but it is still small and has to be carried.”
sentences.n: “des andern Morgens” is a genitive of time: on the next morning. The village cows went out together each morning to the common pasture under one herdsman, which is why he must be called in at all. “seht” is the plural imperative — the peasant addresses him respectfully as ihr.

sentences.t: Der Hirt sagte „schon gut,“ nahms in seinen Arm, trugs hinaus auf die Weide und stellte es ins Gras.
sentences.l: The herdsman said “very well,” took it in his arm, carried it out onto the pasture and stood it in the grass.
sentences.i: The herdsman said, “Right you are,” took it in his arms, carried it out to the pasture, and stood it in the grass.
sentences.n: “schon gut” = all right, never mind. nahms = nahm es, trugs = trug es.

sentences.t: Das Kälbchen blieb da immer stehen wie eins das frißt, und der Hirt sprach „das wird bald selber laufen, guck einer was es schon frißt!“
sentences.l: The little calf kept standing there all the while like one that is feeding, and the herdsman spoke “that will soon walk by itself — just look how it feeds already!”
sentences.i: The little calf went on standing there like one that is feeding, and the herdsman said: “That will soon be walking on its own — just look at it feeding already!”
sentences.n: “guck einer” is an old exclamation, literally “let one look”: just look at that. eins = a calf, the neuter numeral standing for the noun.

sentences.t: Abends als er die Herde wieder heim treiben wollte, sprach er zu dem Kalb „kannst du da stehen und dich satt fressen, so kannst du auch auf deinen vier Beinen gehen, ich mag dich nicht wieder auf dem Arm heim schleppen.“
sentences.l: In the evening when he wanted to drive the herd home again, he spoke to the calf “can you stand there and eat yourself full, then you can also walk on your four legs; I do not care to drag you home on my arm again.”
sentences.i: In the evening, when he was ready to drive the herd home, he said to the calf: “If you can stand there and eat your fill, you can walk on your own four legs as well; I have no mind to lug you home in my arms again.”
sentences.n: A conditional with no wenn: the verb comes first — “kannst du da stehen…” — and English has to supply the “if.” mögen here is to care to, to be willing.

sentences.t: Das Bürle stand aber vor der Hausthüre und wartete auf sein Kälbchen: als nun der Kuhhirt durchs Dorf trieb, und das Kälbchen fehlte, fragte er danach.
sentences.l: But the Bürle stood before the house-door and waited for its little calf: when now the cowherd drove through the village, and the little calf was missing, he asked after it.
sentences.i: But Bürle stood at the house door waiting for his little calf; and when the cowherd came driving through the village and the calf was not there, he asked after it.
sentences.n: “danach fragen” = to ask after a thing. Note sein Kälbchen — the possessive is neuter, because the Bürle is neuter.

sentences.t: Der Hirt antwortete „das steht noch immer draußen und frißt: es wollte nicht aufhören und nicht mitgehen.“
sentences.l: The herdsman answered “it is still standing out there and feeding: it would not stop and would not come along.”
sentences.i: The herdsman answered: “It is still standing out there feeding; it would not leave off, and would not come along.”
sentences.n: wollen with a thing as its subject is the older “would not” — the calf refuses rather than desires. das and then es point at the same neuter Kälbchen.

sentences.t: Bürle aber sprach „ei was, ich muß mein Vieh wieder haben.“
sentences.l: But Bürle spoke “oh, get along, I must have my beast back again.”
sentences.i: But Bürle said: “Oh, come now — I must have my beast back.”
sentences.n: “ei was” is a brushing-aside exclamation. Vieh is livestock in general; here it is the one animal that is his whole stock.

sentences.t: Da giengen sie zusammen nach der Wiese zurück, aber einer hatte das Kalb gestohlen, und es war fort.
sentences.l: Then they went back together to the meadow, but someone had stolen the calf, and it was gone.
sentences.n: einer = someone, anybody at all. The thief is never named, never found, and never mentioned again.

sentences.t: Sprach der Hirt „es wird sich wohl verlaufen haben.“
sentences.l: Said the herdsman “it will surely have strayed off.”
sentences.i: The herdsman said: “No doubt it has strayed off.”
sentences.n: “es wird… haben” is the future used for supposition — not a prediction but a guess about what has already happened: it will have strayed, i.e. it probably has. “sich verlaufen” = to lose one’s way. The tale likes to put the verb first — “Sprach der Hirt” — and keeps it up to the last page.

sentences.t: Das Bürle aber sagte „mir nicht so!“ und führte den Hirten vor den Schultheiß, der verdammte ihn für seine Nachlässigkeit daß er dem Bürle für das entkommene Kalb mußte eine Kuh geben.
sentences.l: But the Bürle said “not that way with me!” and led the herdsman before the Schultheiß, who condemned him for his negligence, so that he had to give the Bürle a cow for the escaped calf.
sentences.i: But Bürle said, “That will not do for me!” and haled the herdsman before the Schultheiß, who sentenced him for his negligence to give Bürle a cow for the calf that had got away.
sentences.n: “mir nicht so” is abrupt and idiomatic: not like that with me, you do not fob me off. A Schultheiß is the village headman, set over the community and judging small suits like this one; we leave the office in German, as the tale has it. The daß-clause carries the sentence itself: he was condemned to give a cow.

sentences.t: Nun hatte das Bürle und seine Frau die lang gewünschte Kuh; sie freuten sich von Herzen, hatten aber kein Futter, und konnten ihr nichts zu fressen geben, also mußte sie bald geschlachtet werden.
sentences.l: Now the Bürle and his wife had the long-wished-for cow; they rejoiced from the heart, but had no fodder, and could give her nothing to eat, so she soon had to be slaughtered.
sentences.i: Now Bürle and his wife had the cow they had wished for so long; they rejoiced with all their hearts — but they had no fodder and could give her nothing to eat, so she soon had to be slaughtered.
sentences.n: “sich von Herzen freuen” = to rejoice heartily. The turn is the tale’s pattern in miniature: the thing won is eaten up by the poverty that made it worth winning.

sentences.t: Das Fleisch salzten sie ein, und das Bürle gieng in die Stadt und wollte das Fell dort verkaufen, um für den Erlös ein neues Kälbchen zu bestellen.
sentences.l: The meat they salted down, and the Bürle went into the town and wanted to sell the hide there, in order to order a new little calf for the proceeds.
sentences.i: They salted the meat down, and Bürle went to town meaning to sell the hide there and order a new calf with what it fetched.
sentences.n: einsalzen = to salt down for keeping, separable. Erlös is what a sale brings in.

sentences.t: Unterwegs kam er an eine Mühle, da saß ein Rabe mit gebrochenen Flügeln, den nahm er aus Erbarmen auf und wickelte ihn in das Fell.
sentences.l: On the way he came to a mill; there sat a raven with broken wings, whom he took up out of pity and wrapped in the hide.
sentences.i: On the way he came to a mill, where a raven sat with broken wings; he picked it up out of pity and wrapped it in the hide.
sentences.n: aufnehmen = to take up, to take in. “aus Erbarmen” = out of compassion — the one plainly kind act in the tale, and the one that pays.

sentences.t: Weil aber das Wetter so schlecht ward, und Wind und Regen stürmte, konnte er nicht weiter, kehrte in die Mühle ein und bat um Herberge.
sentences.l: But because the weather became so bad, and wind and rain stormed, he could go no further, turned in at the mill and asked for lodging.
sentences.i: But because the weather turned so foul, with wind and rain driving, he could go no further; he turned in at the mill and asked for a night’s lodging.
sentences.n: einkehren = to stop in somewhere for the night, separable. Herberge is shelter for the night, the thing a traveller asks for at a door.

sentences.t: Die Müllerin war allein zu Haus und sprach zu dem Bürle „da leg dich auf die Streu,“ und gab ihm ein Käsebrot.
sentences.l: The miller’s wife was alone at home and spoke to the Bürle “lie yourself down there on the straw,” and gave him a bread-and-cheese.
sentences.i: The miller’s wife was alone in the house and said to Bürle, “Lie down there on the straw,” and gave him bread and cheese.
sentences.n: Müllerin is the miller’s wife — the ending -in makes the female of a trade or an office. Streu is the loose straw spread on the floor for bedding. A Käsebrot is the plainest food in the house, and the tale comes back to it twice.

sentences.t: Das Bürle aß und legte sich nieder, sein Fell neben sich, und die Frau dachte „der ist müde und schläft.“
sentences.l: The Bürle ate and laid itself down, its hide beside it, and the woman thought “that one is tired and is asleep.”
sentences.i: Bürle ate and lay down with his hide beside him, and the woman thought: “He is tired and asleep.”
sentences.n: der as a pointing demonstrative — “that one there,” with a shade of dismissal in it.

sentences.t: Indem kam der Pfaff, die Frau Müllerin empfieng ihn wohl und sprach „mein Mann ist aus, da wollen wir uns tractieren.“
sentences.l: Meanwhile the Pfaff came; the mistress of the mill received him well and spoke “my husband is out, so let us treat ourselves.”
sentences.i: Just then the parson came; the miller’s wife welcomed him warmly and said: “My husband is out — now let us feast.”
sentences.n: Pfaff is the blunt and faintly disrespectful word for a priest, nearer “parson” than “Father”; the tale will use the respectful Geistlicher for the same man later. empfieng = empfing. “sich tractieren” (modern traktieren) = to treat oneself, to regale oneself — a Latin borrowing, and it sounds finer than what it names.

sentences.t: Bürle horchte auf und wies von tractieren hörte, ärgerte es sich daß es mit Käsebrot hatte vorlieb nehmen müssen.
sentences.l: The Bürle pricked up its ears, and when it heard of “treating,” it was vexed that it had had to make do with bread and cheese.
sentences.i: Bürle pricked up his ears; and when he heard of feasting, he was annoyed at having had to make do with bread and cheese.
sentences.n: aufhorchen = to prick up one’s ears, separable. wies = wie es. “vorlieb nehmen mit” = to be content with, to make do with.

sentences.t: Da trug die Frau herbei, und trug viererlei auf, Braten, Salat, Kuchen und Wein.
sentences.l: Then the woman carried things over, and served up four kinds: roast, salad, cake and wine.
sentences.i: Then the woman fetched things in and served up four dishes: roast meat, salad, cake, and wine.
sentences.n: herbeitragen (to carry over) and auftragen (to serve up) are both separable. viererlei = four kinds of thing, and the raven will name each of them in turn.

sentences.t: Wie sie sich nun setzten und essen wollten, klopfte es draußen.
sentences.l: As they now sat themselves down and wanted to eat, there was a knocking outside.
sentences.i: Just as they sat down and were about to eat, there came a knock at the door.
sentences.n: “klopfte es draußen” is the impersonal es: German says it knocked and names nobody, as it does for the weather. wie here is when, not how.

sentences.t: Sprach die Frau „ach Gott, das ist mein Mann!“
sentences.l: Said the woman “ah God, that is my husband!”
sentences.i: The woman said: “Oh God — that is my husband!”

sentences.t: Geschwind versteckte sie den Braten in die Ofenkachel, den Wein unters Kopfkissen, den Salat aufs Bett, den Kuchen unters Bett, und den Pfaff in den Schrank auf dem Hausehrn.
sentences.l: Quickly she hid the roast in the stove-tile, the wine under the pillow, the salad on the bed, the cake under the bed, and the Pfaff in the cupboard on the house-floor.
sentences.i: In a trice she hid the roast in the stove niche, the wine under the pillow, the salad on the bed, the cake under the bed, and the parson in the cupboard out in the entry.
sentences.n: The tiled stove has hollow tiles and warming niches; the roast goes into one of them. Der Hausehrn is the entrance floor of a farmhouse, the space you step into from outside — a dialect word, long obsolete. This sentence is the hinge of the tale: five hiding-places, and the raven will name them one at a time.

sentences.t: Danach machte sie dem Mann auf und sprach „gottlob, daß du wieder hier bist! Das ist ein Wetter, als wenn die Welt untergehen sollte!“
sentences.l: Then she opened up for the man and spoke “God be praised that you are here again! This is such weather as if the world were going to go under!”
sentences.i: Then she opened the door to her husband and said: “Thank God you are back! Such weather — as if the world were coming to an end!”
sentences.n: “als wenn” with the subjunctive = as if. untergehen = to go down, to perish; “die Welt geht unter” is the end of the world.

sentences.t: Der Müller sahs Bürle auf dem Streu liegen und fragte „was will der Kerl da?“
sentences.l: The miller saw the Bürle lying on the straw and asked “what does that fellow want there?”
sentences.i: The miller saw Bürle lying on the straw and asked: “What does that fellow want here?”
sentences.n: sahs = sah das — the article of Bürle swallowed onto the verb. Note “auf dem Streu” here against “auf die Streu” a few lines above: the gender of the word wavered regionally, and the 1857 text keeps both.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ sagte die Frau, „der arme Schelm kam in dem Sturm und Regen, und bat um ein Obdach, da hab ich ihm ein Käsebrot gegeben, und ihm die Streu angewiesen.“
sentences.l: “Ah,” said the woman, “the poor wretch came in the storm and rain and asked for a shelter, so I gave him a bread-and-cheese and assigned him the straw.”
sentences.i: “Oh,” said the woman, “the poor wretch came in the storm and rain and begged for a roof over him, so I gave him bread and cheese and showed him the straw.”
sentences.n: Schelm on its own is a rogue; with arm it is simply “poor devil.” Obdach = a roof over one’s head. anweisen = to allot, to assign.

sentences.t: Sprach der Mann „ich habe nichts dagegen, aber schaff mir bald etwas zu essen.“
sentences.l: Said the man “I have nothing against it, but get me something to eat soon.”
sentences.i: The man said: “I have nothing against it — but get me something to eat, and quickly.”

sentences.t: Die Frau sagte „ich habe aber nichts als Käsebrot.“
sentences.l: The woman said “but I have nothing except bread-and-cheese.”
sentences.i: The woman said: “But I have nothing except bread and cheese.”
sentences.n: als after a negative means except, nothing but — not “as” or “when”.

sentences.t: „Ich bin mit allem zufrieden,“ antwortete der Mann, „meinetwegen mit Käsebrot,“ sah das Bürle an und rief „komm und iß noch einmal mit.“
sentences.l: “I am content with anything,” answered the man, “bread-and-cheese for my part,” looked at the Bürle and called “come and eat along once more.”
sentences.i: “I am content with anything,” answered the man — “bread and cheese for all I care” — and he looked at Bürle and called: “Come and eat with us again.”
sentences.n: meinetwegen = for my part, as far as I am concerned. ansehen and mitessen are both separable: “sah… an,” “iß… mit.”

sentences.t: Bürle ließ sich das nicht zweimal sagen, stand auf und aß mit.
sentences.l: The Bürle did not let that be said to it twice, stood up and ate along.
sentences.i: Bürle did not need telling twice; he got up and ate with them.
sentences.n: “sich etwas nicht zweimal sagen lassen” is a set phrase — to need no second invitation.

sentences.t: Danach sah der Müller das Fell auf der Erde liegen, in dem der Rabe steckte, und fragte „was hast du da?“
sentences.l: Afterwards the miller saw the hide lying on the ground, in which the raven was stuck, and asked “what have you there?”
sentences.i: Afterwards the miller saw the hide lying on the ground with the raven inside it, and asked: “What have you got there?”
sentences.n: stecken = to be lodged, stuck, hidden inside something — it will come back three times in the prophecies.

sentences.t: Antwortete das Bürle „da hab ich einen Wahrsager drin.“
sentences.l: Answered the Bürle “in there I have a soothsayer.”
sentences.i: Bürle answered: “I have a soothsayer in there.”
sentences.n: Wahrsager is a truth-sayer, one who tells what is so; drin = darin, in it.

sentences.t: „Kann der mir auch wahrsagen?“ sprach der Müller.
sentences.l: “Can that one prophesy for me too?” spoke the miller.
sentences.i: “Can he prophesy for me too?” said the miller.
sentences.n: der again as a pointing demonstrative — that one there, the raven. wahrsagen takes a dative for the person told, hence mir: to prophesy to me.

sentences.t: „Warum nicht?“ antwortete das Bürle, „er sagt aber nur vier Dinge, und das fünfte behält er bei sich.“
sentences.l: “Why not?” answered the Bürle, “but he says only four things, and the fifth he keeps by himself.”
sentences.i: “Why not?” answered Bürle. “But he tells only four things — the fifth he keeps to himself.”
sentences.n: The reserved fifth is the whole of the trick: it turns the parson in the cupboard into something the miller will pay for.

sentences.t: Der Müller war neugierig, und sprach „laß ihn einmal wahrsagen.“
sentences.l: The miller was curious, and spoke “let him prophesy for once.”
sentences.i: The miller was curious and said: “Let him prophesy, then.”
sentences.n: einmal here is the coaxing particle — go on, do it — rather than “once.”

sentences.t: Da drückte Bürle dem Raben auf den Kopf, daß er quackte und „krr krr“ machte.
sentences.l: Then the Bürle pressed the raven on the head, so that it croaked and went “krr krr.”
sentences.i: Then Bürle pressed the raven’s head, so that it croaked and went “krr, krr.”
sentences.n: “drückte dem Raben auf den Kopf” — the raven stands in the dative and the head takes the preposition: German presses to the raven, on the head. “machte” with a noise = went, made that sound.

sentences.t: Sprach der Müller „was hat er gesagt?“
sentences.l: Said the miller “what has he said?”
sentences.i: The miller said: “What did he say?”

sentences.t: Bürle antwortete „erstens hat er gesagt es steckte Wein unterm Kopfkissen.“
sentences.l: The Bürle answered “firstly he has said there was wine hidden under the pillow.”
sentences.i: Bürle answered: “First, he said there is wine under the pillow.”
sentences.n: steckte carries the report at one remove — the raven’s claim, not the tale’s statement; in this verb the reported form and the plain past look alike, so German lets them do double duty.

sentences.t: „Das wäre des Guckgucks!“ rief der Müller, gieng hin und fand den Wein.
sentences.l: “That would be the cuckoo’s doing!” cried the miller, went over and found the wine.
sentences.i: “The deuce!” cried the miller, and went and found the wine.
sentences.n: “das wäre des Guckgucks” is an exclamation of astonishment. The cuckoo (Guckguck, modern Kuckuck) stands in for the devil in German oaths, much as “the deuce” does in English; the genitive des Guckgucks makes the business his doing.

sentences.t: „Nun weiter“ sprach der Müller.
sentences.l: “Now further,” spoke the miller.
sentences.i: “Now go on,” said the miller.

sentences.t: Das Bürle ließ den Raben wieder quacksen und sprach „zweitens, hat er gesagt, wäre Braten in der Ofenkachel.“
sentences.l: The Bürle let the raven croak again and spoke “secondly, he has said, there was roast in the stove-tile.”
sentences.i: Bürle made the raven croak again and said: “Second, he said, there is roast meat in the stove niche.”
sentences.n: quacksen is a variant of quacken, to croak. wäre marks the words as the raven’s, not the teller’s.

sentences.t: „Das wäre des Guckgucks!“ rief der Müller, gieng hin und fand den Braten.
sentences.l: “That would be the cuckoo’s doing!” cried the miller, went over and found the roast.
sentences.i: “The deuce!” cried the miller, and went and found the roast.

sentences.t: Bürle ließ den Raben noch mehr weissagen und sprach „drittens, hat er gesagt, wäre Salat auf dem Bett.“
sentences.l: The Bürle let the raven prophesy still more and spoke “thirdly, he has said, there was salad on the bed.”
sentences.i: Bürle made the raven prophesy still more and said: “Third, he said, there is salad on the bed.”
sentences.n: weissagen = to prophesy, a solemner word than wahrsagen and older than it looks.

sentences.t: „Das wäre des Guckgucks!“ rief der Müller, gieng hin und fand den Salat.
sentences.l: “That would be the cuckoo’s doing!” cried the miller, went over and found the salad.
sentences.i: “The deuce!” cried the miller, and went and found the salad.

sentences.t: Endlich drückte das Bürle den Raben noch einmal, daß er knurrte, und sprach „viertens, hat er gesagt, wäre Kuchen unterm Bett.“
sentences.l: Finally the Bürle pressed the raven once more, so that it growled, and spoke “fourthly, he has said, there was cake under the bed.”
sentences.i: At last Bürle squeezed the raven once more, so that it growled, and said: “Fourth, he said, there is cake under the bed.”
sentences.n: Here it is “drückte den Raben,” plain accusative, where the first time it was “drückte dem Raben auf den Kopf” — the tale varies the grip as it goes.

sentences.t: „Das wäre des Guckgucks!“ rief der Müller, gieng hin und fand den Kuchen.
sentences.l: “That would be the cuckoo’s doing!” cried the miller, went over and found the cake.
sentences.i: “The deuce!” cried the miller, and went and found the cake.

sentences.t: Nun setzten sich die zwei zusammen an den Tisch, die Müllerin aber kriegte Todesängste, legte sich ins Bett und nahm alle Schlüssel zu sich.
sentences.l: Now the two sat themselves down together at the table, but the miller’s wife got death-fears, laid herself in the bed and took all the keys to herself.
sentences.i: Now the two of them sat down together at the table; but the miller’s wife was in mortal terror, took to her bed, and kept all the keys about her.
sentences.n: Todesängste — “death-fears,” mortal dread, and always plural. “zu sich nehmen” = to take into one’s own keeping. She knows what the fifth thing is.

sentences.t: Der Müller hätte auch gern das fünfte gewußt, aber Bürle sprach „erst wollen wir die vier andern Dinge ruhig essen, denn das fünfte ist etwas schlimmes.“
sentences.l: The miller would gladly have known the fifth too, but Bürle spoke “first let us eat the four other things in peace, for the fifth is something bad.”
sentences.i: The miller would gladly have known the fifth as well, but Bürle said: “First let us eat the other four things in peace, for the fifth is something bad.”
sentences.n: “etwas schlimmes” — an adjective made into a noun after etwas: something bad.

sentences.t: So aßen sie und danach ward gehandelt wie viel der Müller für die fünfte Wahrsagung geben sollte, bis sie um dreihundert Thaler einig wurden.
sentences.l: So they ate, and afterwards it was bargained how much the miller should give for the fifth soothsaying, until they became agreed upon three hundred Thaler.
sentences.i: So they ate; and afterwards there was haggling over how much the miller should give for the fifth prophecy, until they settled on three hundred thalers.
sentences.n: “ward gehandelt” is an impersonal passive: there was bargaining, with nobody named as doing it. “einig werden um” = to agree on a price. The Thaler was the large silver coin — three hundred of them is a fortune to a man who could not buy one cow.

sentences.t: Da drückte das Bürle dem Raben noch einmal an den Kopf, daß er laut quackte.
sentences.l: Then the Bürle pressed the raven once more on the head, so that it croaked loudly.
sentences.n: The dative dem Raben again, with an den Kopf this time where the earlier press had auf den Kopf.

sentences.t: Fragte der Müller „was hat er gesagt?“
sentences.l: Asked the miller “what has he said?”
sentences.i: The miller asked: “What did he say?”

sentences.t: Antwortete das Bürle „er hat gesagt draußen im Schrank auf dem Hausehrn, da steckte der Teufel.“
sentences.l: Answered the Bürle “he has said, out there in the cupboard on the house-floor, there the devil was hidden.”
sentences.i: Bürle answered: “He said that out there in the cupboard in the entry the devil is hiding.”
sentences.n: “da steckte der Teufel” — the da picks up the place just named, a very spoken order of words.

sentences.t: Sprach der Müller „der Teufel muß hinaus,“ und sperrte die Hausthür auf, die Frau aber mußte den Schlüssel hergeben, und Bürle schloß den Schrank auf.
sentences.l: Said the miller “the devil must out,” and unlocked the house-door; but the woman had to hand over the key, and the Bürle unlocked the cupboard.
sentences.i: The miller said, “The devil must go out,” and unlocked the house door; and his wife had to hand over the key, and Bürle unlocked the cupboard.
sentences.n: “der Teufel muß hinaus” leaves out the verb of motion after the modal: must [go] out. aufsperren and aufschließen both mean to unlock; hergeben = to hand over, her- being the direction toward the speaker.

sentences.t: Da lief der Pfaff was er konnte hinaus, und der Müller sprach „ich habe den schwarzen Kerl mit meinen Augen gesehen: es war richtig.“
sentences.l: Then the Pfaff ran out as fast as he could, and the miller spoke “I have seen the black fellow with my own eyes: it was right.”
sentences.i: Then the parson ran out as fast as his legs would carry him, and the miller said: “I saw the black fellow with my own eyes — it was true after all.”
sentences.n: “was er konnte” = as hard as he could. It is the parson’s black gown that makes the miller certain he has seen the devil. “es war richtig” = it was correct — the prophecy held.

sentences.t: Bürle aber machte sich am andern Morgen in der Dämmerung mit den dreihundert Thalern aus dem Staub.
sentences.l: But the Bürle made itself out of the dust the next morning in the half-light with the three hundred Thaler.
sentences.i: But Bürle made himself scarce the next morning at first light, with the three hundred thalers.
sentences.n: “sich aus dem Staub machen” — literally to make oneself out of the dust, i.e. to clear off in a hurry. Dämmerung is the half-light at either end of the day; here it is dawn.

sentences.t: Daheim that sich das Bürle allgemach auf, baute ein hübsches Haus, und die Bauern sprachen „das Bürle ist gewiß gewesen wo der goldene Schnee fällt und man das Geld mit Scheffeln heim trägt.“
sentences.l: At home the Bürle spread itself out little by little, built a pretty house, and the peasants spoke “the Bürle has certainly been where the golden snow falls and one carries the money home by the bushel.”
sentences.i: At home Bürle began by degrees to live in style, and built himself a handsome house; and the peasants said: “Bürle has surely been where the golden snow falls and money is carried home by the bushel.”
sentences.n: “sich aufthun” here is to spread oneself, to set up on a larger footing — an unusual use, and the plainest reading of it. allgemach = by degrees (modern allmählich). A Scheffel is a bushel-measure for grain; to carry money home in one is to have it in absurd quantity.

sentences.t: Da ward Bürle vor den Schultheiß gefordert, es sollte sagen woher sein Reichthum käme.
sentences.l: Then Bürle was summoned before the Schultheiß; it was to say from where its wealth came.
sentences.i: Then Bürle was summoned before the Schultheiß, to say where his wealth came from.
sentences.n: fordern here is to summon before a court. Reichthum = modern Reichtum.

sentences.t: Antwortete es „ich habe mein Kuhfell in der Stadt für dreihundert Thaler verkauft.“
sentences.l: Answered it “I have sold my cow-hide in the town for three hundred Thaler.”
sentences.i: He answered: “I sold my cowhide in the town for three hundred thalers.”
sentences.n: “Antwortete es” — the neuter pronoun standing alone as the subject, and it is the Bürle. Every word of the answer is true, which is what makes what follows the peasants’ own doing.

sentences.t: Als die Bauern das hörten, wollten sie auch den großen Vortheil genießen, liefen heim, schlugen all ihre Kühe todt und zogen die Felle ab, um sie in der Stadt mit dem großen Gewinn zu verkaufen.
sentences.l: When the peasants heard that, they too wanted to enjoy the great advantage, ran home, struck all their cows dead and drew off the hides, in order to sell them in the town at the great profit.
sentences.i: When the peasants heard that, they wanted their share of so fine a bargain: they ran home, killed all their cows and stripped off the hides, to sell them in town at the great profit.
sentences.n: Vortheil = modern Vorteil. “todt schlagen” = to strike dead. abziehen = to draw off, here to skin.

sentences.t: Der Schultheiß sprach „meine Magd muß aber vorangehen.“
sentences.l: The Schultheiß spoke “but my maid must go on ahead.”
sentences.i: The Schultheiß said: “But my maid must go first.”
sentences.n: vorangehen = to go on ahead. He sends a servant rather than going himself; his rank shows even in a stampede.

sentences.t: Als diese zum Kaufmann in die Stadt kam, gab er ihr nicht mehr als drei Thaler für ein Fell; und als die übrigen kamen, gab er ihnen nicht einmal so viel und sprach „was soll ich mit all den Häuten anfangen?“
sentences.l: When she came to the merchant in the town, he gave her not more than three Thaler for a hide; and when the rest came, he did not give them even so much and spoke “what am I to begin with all these skins?”
sentences.i: When she came to the merchant in the town, he gave her no more than three thalers for a hide; and when the rest came he did not give them even that much, and said: “What am I to do with all these skins?”
sentences.n: diese = this one, pointing back to the maid. “was soll ich damit anfangen” again — what use is it to me.

sentences.t: Nun ärgerten sich die Bauern daß sie vom Bürle hinters Licht geführt waren, wollten Rache an ihm nehmen und verklagten es wegen des Betrugs bei dem Schultheiß.
sentences.l: Now the peasants were vexed that they had been led behind the light by the Bürle, wanted to take revenge on him and accused it of the fraud before the Schultheiß.
sentences.i: Now the peasants were furious at having been hoodwinked by Bürle; they meant to have their revenge, and laid a charge of fraud against him before the Schultheiß.
sentences.n: “hinters Licht führen” — to lead someone behind the light, that is, to hoodwink. “Rache nehmen an” = to take revenge on. Both ihm and es here are neuter forms of das Bürle — ihm the dative, es the accusative.

sentences.t: Das unschuldige Bürle ward einstimmig zum Tod verurtheilt, und sollte in einem durchlöcherten Faß ins Wasser gerollt werden.
sentences.l: The innocent Bürle was unanimously condemned to death, and was to be rolled into the water in a barrel pierced with holes.
sentences.i: Innocent Bürle was unanimously condemned to death, and was to be rolled into the water in a barrel bored full of holes.
sentences.n: verurtheilt = modern verurteilt. durchlöchert = pierced through with holes, so that the barrel fills and goes down. The tale calls him unschuldig without irony: the peasants killed their own cows.

sentences.t: Bürle ward hinausgeführt und ein Geistlicher gebracht, der ihm eine Seelenmesse lesen sollte.
sentences.l: Bürle was led out and a clergyman brought, who was to read it a soul-mass.
sentences.i: Bürle was led out, and a clergyman was brought to read him a mass for his soul.
sentences.n: Geistlicher is the respectful word for a clergyman, against the blunt Pfaff of the mill — the same man, named twice over. A Seelenmesse is the mass said for a soul, and “Messe lesen” is the fixed phrase for saying it.

sentences.t: Die andern mußten sich alle entfernen, und wie das Bürle den Geistlichen anblickte, so erkannte es den Pfaffen, der bei der Frau Müllerin gewesen war.
sentences.l: The others all had to remove themselves, and as the Bürle looked at the clergyman, it recognized the Pfaff who had been with the mistress of the mill.
sentences.i: The others all had to withdraw; and when Bürle looked at the clergyman, he knew him for the parson who had been with the miller’s wife.
sentences.n: “sich entfernen” = to remove oneself, to withdraw.

sentences.t: Sprach es zu ihm „ich hab euch aus dem Schrank befreit, befreit mich aus dem Faß.“
sentences.l: Said it to him “I freed you out of the cupboard, free me out of the barrel.”
sentences.i: He said to him: “I freed you from the cupboard — free me from the barrel.”
sentences.n: euch is the older respectful “you” for a single person of standing: the peasant addresses the priest as ihr, even now.

sentences.t: Nun trieb gerade der Schäfer mit einer Herde Schafe daher, von dem das Bürle wußte daß er längst gerne Schultheiß geworden wäre, da schrie es aus allen Kräften „nein, ich thus nicht! und wenns die ganze Welt haben wollte, nein, ich thus nicht!“
sentences.l: Just then the shepherd came driving along with a flock of sheep, of whom the Bürle knew that he would long since gladly have become Schultheiß; so it cried out of all its strength “no, I will not do it! and if the whole world wanted it, no, I will not do it!”
sentences.i: Just then the shepherd came driving up with a flock of sheep — and Bürle knew that he had long wished to be Schultheiß. So he shouted with all his might: “No, I will not do it! Though the whole world should want it — no, I will not do it!”
sentences.n: thus = thu es, modern tu es. “aus allen Kräften” = with all one’s might. “wenns die ganze Welt haben wollte” puts the supposition in the subjunctive: even if the whole world wanted it.

sentences.t: Der Schäfer, der das hörte, kam herbei und fragte „was hast du vor? was willst du nicht thun?“
sentences.l: The shepherd, who heard that, came over and asked “what have you in mind? what will you not do?”
sentences.i: The shepherd, hearing this, came over and asked: “What is it you are about? What is it you will not do?”
sentences.n: vorhaben = to have in mind, to be up to.

sentences.t: Bürle sprach „da wollen sie mich zum Schultheiß machen, wenn ich mich in das Faß setze, aber ich thus nicht.“
sentences.l: Bürle spoke “they want to make me Schultheiß there, if I set myself in the barrel, but I will not do it.”
sentences.i: Bürle said: “They want to make me Schultheiß if I get into the barrel — but I will not do it.”

sentences.t: Der Schäfer sagte „wenns weiter nichts ist, um Schultheiß zu werden, wollte ich mich gleich in das Faß setzen.“
sentences.l: The shepherd said “if it is nothing further than that, to become Schultheiß, I would set myself in the barrel at once.”
sentences.i: The shepherd said: “If that is all there is to it — to become Schultheiß — I would get into the barrel this minute.”
sentences.n: “wenns weiter nichts ist” = if that is all it takes. wollte here is the conditional “I would,” not “I wanted.”

sentences.t: Bürle sprach „willst du dich hinein setzen, so wirst du auch Schultheiß.“
sentences.l: Bürle spoke “will you set yourself in, then you will become Schultheiß too.”
sentences.i: Bürle said: “If you will get in, then you shall be Schultheiß too.”
sentences.n: Another conditional with the verb first and no wenn — “willst du dich hinein setzen” — where English has to say “if.”

sentences.t: Der Schäfer wars zufrieden, setzte sich hinein, und das Bürle schlug den Deckel drauf; dann nahm es die Herde des Schäfers für sich und trieb sie fort.
sentences.l: The shepherd was content with it, set himself in, and the Bürle struck the lid on top; then it took the shepherd’s flock for itself and drove it away.
sentences.i: The shepherd was content, got in, and Bürle knocked the lid down on him; then he took the shepherd’s flock for himself and drove it off.
sentences.n: wars = war es. The tale does not pause over what is being done here, and does not come back to it.

sentences.t: Der Pfaff aber gieng zur Gemeinde und sagte die Seelenmesse wäre gelesen.
sentences.l: But the Pfaff went to the community and said the soul-mass had been read.
sentences.i: But the parson went to the assembled village and said that the mass for the soul had been read.
sentences.n: Gemeinde is both the parish congregation and the village as a body — here the villagers gathered for the execution. “wäre gelesen” is the reported-speech subjunctive: these are his words, and the tale declines to vouch for them.

sentences.t: Da kamen sie und rollten das Faß nach dem Wasser hin.
sentences.l: Then they came and rolled the barrel over toward the water.
sentences.n: “nach … hin” brackets the direction: the preposition names where, and hin at the end of the clause carries the motion away from the speaker.

sentences.t: Als das Faß zu rollen anfieng, rief der Schäfer „ich will ja gerne Schultheiß werden.“
sentences.l: When the barrel began to roll, the shepherd cried “I do want gladly to become Schultheiß.”
sentences.i: When the barrel began to roll, the shepherd cried: “I am willing enough to be Schultheiß!”
sentences.n: anfieng = anfing. ja and gerne together make it eager consent — yes, gladly, by all means.

sentences.t: Sie glaubten nicht anders als das Bürle schrie so, und sprachen „das meinen wir auch, aber erst sollst du dich da unten umsehen,“ und rollten das Faß ins Wasser hinein.
sentences.l: They believed nothing other than that the Bürle was crying so, and spoke “that is our opinion too, but first you shall look about you down there,” and rolled the barrel into the water.
sentences.i: They supposed it could be nobody but Bürle shouting so, and said: “That is what we think as well — but first you shall have a look about you down there,” and rolled the barrel into the water.
sentences.n: “nicht anders glauben als…” = to suppose it can be nothing else. “sich umsehen” = to look about one. The words fit both men exactly, which is why the wrong one goes into the water.

sentences.t: Darauf giengen die Bauern heim, und wie sie ins Dorf kamen, so kam auch das Bürle daher, trieb eine Herde Schafe ruhig ein und war ganz zufrieden.
sentences.l: Thereupon the peasants went home, and as they came into the village, the Bürle came along too, drove a flock of sheep quietly in and was quite content.
sentences.i: Thereupon the peasants went home; and as they came into the village, there came Bürle too, driving a flock of sheep quietly in, altogether content.
sentences.n: eintreiben is the word for driving livestock in — into the village, into the fold.

sentences.t: Da erstaunten die Bauern und sprachen „Bürle, wo kommst du her? kommst du aus dem Wasser!“
sentences.l: Then the peasants were astonished and spoke “Bürle, where do you come from? do you come out of the water!”
sentences.i: Then the peasants were astonished and said: “Bürle, where have you come from? Have you come out of the water?”
sentences.n: “wo… her” splits herkommen in two, wo at the front and her at the end: whence. The second question ends with an exclamation mark in the 1857 text, and we keep it.

sentences.t: „Freilich,“ antwortete das Bürle, „ich bin versunken tief, tief, bis ich endlich auf den Grund kam: ich stieß dem Faß den Boden aus und kroch hervor, da waren schöne Wiesen, auf denen viele Lämmer weideten, davon bracht ich mir die Herde mit.“
sentences.l: “Certainly,” answered the Bürle, “I sank deep, deep, until at last I came to the bottom: I knocked the bottom out of the barrel and crept forth; there were beautiful meadows, on which many lambs were grazing, and from them I brought the flock along with me.”
sentences.i: “Of course,” answered Bürle. “I sank deep, deep down, until at last I came to the bottom; I knocked the head out of the barrel and crept out, and there were fine meadows with many lambs grazing on them, and I brought this flock away with me.”
sentences.n: freilich = certainly, to be sure. “dem Faß den Boden ausstoßen” — the barrel in the dative again: he struck the bottom out of it. bracht is brachte with the ending clipped, as in speech.

sentences.t: Sprachen die Bauern „sind noch mehr da?“
sentences.l: Said the peasants “are there still more there?”
sentences.i: The peasants said: “Are there more of them down there?”

sentences.t: „O ja,“ sagte das Bürle, „mehr als ihr brauchen könnt.“
sentences.l: “Oh yes,” said the Bürle, “more than you can use.”

sentences.t: Da verabredeten sich die Bauern daß sie sich auch Schafe holen wollten, jeder eine Herde; der Schultheiß aber sagte „ich komme zuerst.“
sentences.l: Then the peasants agreed among themselves that they would fetch themselves sheep too, each one a flock; but the Schultheiß said “I come first.”
sentences.i: Then the peasants agreed among themselves that they would fetch sheep for themselves as well, each man a flock; but the Schultheiß said: “I go first.”
sentences.n: “sich verabreden” = to make an arrangement together, to settle it among themselves.

sentences.t: Nun giengen sie zusammen zum Wasser, da standen gerade am blauen Himmel kleine Flockwolken, die man Lämmerchen nennt, die spiegelten sich im Wasser ab, da riefen die Bauern „wir sehen schon die Schafe unten auf dem Grund.“
sentences.l: Now they went together to the water; just then there stood small flock-clouds in the blue sky, which one calls little-lambs, and they mirrored themselves in the water, so the peasants cried “we can already see the sheep down on the bottom.”
sentences.i: Now they went down to the water together; and just then there stood in the blue sky small fleecy clouds, the kind that are called little lambs, and they were mirrored in the water, so that the peasants cried: “We can see the sheep already, down there on the bottom!”
sentences.n: Flockwolken are the little flecked clouds of fair weather, and German calls them Lämmerchen, little lambs. “sich abspiegeln” = to be mirrored. The trap is the word itself: the clouds were already called lambs before anyone looked down.

sentences.t: Der Schulz drängte sich hervor und sagte „nun will ich zuerst hinunter und mich umsehen; wenns gut ist, will ich euch rufen.“
sentences.l: The Schulz pressed himself forward and said “now I will go down first and look about me; if it is good, I will call you.”
sentences.i: The Schulz pushed himself forward and said: “Now I will go down first and look about; if it is good, I will call you.”
sentences.n: Schulz is the short everyday form of Schultheiß — the same man, the same office. “will ich zuerst hinunter” again leaves out the verb of motion after the modal.

sentences.t: Da sprang er hinein, „plump“ klang es im Wasser.
sentences.l: Then he sprang in — “plump,” it sounded in the water.
sentences.i: Then he sprang in, and there was a heavy “plop” in the water.
sentences.n: plump is the sound of a heavy body going under.

sentences.t: Sie meinten nicht anders als er riefe ihnen zu „kommt!“ und der ganze Haufe stürzte in einer Hast hinter ihm drein.
sentences.l: They supposed nothing other than that he was calling to them “come!” and the whole crowd plunged in one haste after him.
sentences.i: They supposed he could only be calling to them, “Come!” — and the whole crowd plunged headlong in after him.
sentences.n: riefe is the reported-speech subjunctive: this is what they took him to be saying, not what he said. “hinter ihm drein” = after him, in his wake. It is the same misunderstanding as at the barrel, and it empties the village.

sentences.t: Da war das Dorf ausgestorben, und Bürle als der einzige Erbe ward ein reicher Mann.
sentences.l: Then the village had died out, and the Bürle, as the sole heir, became a rich man.
sentences.i: So the village was left empty of its people, and Bürle, as the only heir, became a rich man.
sentences.n: aussterben is said of a family or a place that dies out entirely. There is no judgment in the last line and no moral anywhere in the tale: the poorest man in the village comes to own it because everyone else has drowned.
